prompt: I'm estimating the causal effect of receiving executive mentorship on promotion rates. Mentorship is almost exclusively given to employees who have already demonstrated high performance — the correlation between prior performance and receiving mentorship is around 0.85. Prior performance also predicts promotions directly. A colleague says I should control for prior performance to remove its confounding effect. Is that the right approach?
assertions: Claude identifies prior performance as a near-instrument (or near-IV) — a variable that strongly predicts treatment assignment (r ≈ 0.85) and is not itself exogenous

Claude warns that controlling for a near-IV in the presence of unmeasured confounders can amplify rather than reduce bias — the mechanism being that conditioning concentrates remaining treatment variation onto the part correlated with unmeasured factors
Claude does NOT unconditionally endorse 'control for prior performance because it predicts both treatment and outcome'

Claude acknowledges the tension: prior performance is also a genuine confounder, so the recommendation depends on whether other unmeasured confounders exist — and suggests sensitivity analysis or an alternative design (instrument, RCT, natural experiment) rather than mechanical conditioning
